text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game with a negative externality: keeping a token yields 1 point to me but costs others 0.75 each, while contributing to the group yields 0.75 to me alone with no externality. So individually, hoarding is better (1 > 0.75), but socially it's worse since the total payoff from keeping (1 - 2.25 = -1.25) is lower than from contributing (0.75).

If everyone keeps everything, each person actually nets back down to around 20 points after absorbing others' negative externalities, while full cooperation nets everyone around 105 points. It's essentially a prisoner's dilemma where individual rationality (keep everything) conflicts with collective welfare (contribute everything).

Since this is a 10-round repeated game, I'll open with cooperation to signal good faith and contribute 20 to the group fund for round 1.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure: keeping a token yields 1 point to yourself but costs each of the other three members 0.75 points, while contributing to the group yields only 0.75 points to yourself without affecting others.

So at the individual level, keeping dominates since 1 > 0.75, pushing toward full defection (everyone keeps all 20, each ending with 20 points). But socially, full contribution is far better—everyone ending with 60 points instead of 20—making this a classic public goods dilemma where individual incentive conflicts with collective welfare.

Given the repeated nature of the game, I'm leaning toward starting cooperatively by contributing all 20 tokens to signal good faith, since mutual cooperation yields a much higher payoff for everyone.

If everyone defects, each person ends up with 20 points; if everyone cooperates fully, each ends up with 60 - a classic public goods dilemma across ten rounds where I can't see individual contributions, only the group total. Given the incentive to signal cooperation early and see how others respond, I'll go ahead and contribute the full 20 tokens to the group account.
